narrative:
The model predicted an 82.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors that strongly signaled a high risk of bar exam failure. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the single biggest reason for the rejection. Being in the bottom decile of your class, compared to an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students, pulled the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and told the same story: you also placed in the bottom decile, far below the typical sixth-decile performance of admitted students. Together, these two academic-standing measures outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score of 28 was the third most influential piece of information. It sits well below the average of 37 among accepted applicants and therefore also pushed the model toward predicting failure.

None of the other details in your profile, including your family income, undergraduate GPA, gender, race, or plan to attend full-time, played a meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and retaking the LSAT to raise your score into a more competitive range. Once those two areas show clear progress, reapply. Many students successfully turn around similar profiles with targeted improvement.
